chapter: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
title: 'Pick Yourself Up' and a famous musician testing him in public
summary: Thompson describes the song's key changes and recalls a well-known jazz musician who challenged him to play it in front of a crowd, which he played badly.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yes, it does. Well, this --
There's a song called 'Pick Yourself Up', incidently.
Is there? I didn't know that.
(Humming of song)
Oh, yes, that's right.
That's a very complicated song to play, would you believe it? It goes through three keys, it goes into four keys.
Does it?

The first part starts off, if you're going to play it for instance in the key -- here's something for you musical people who might know something about chord changes. Here's a little lesson for you from a jazz musician. I also sometimes have called chase, c-h-a-s-e. Do you know how I got that name? Because I used to sign my name C-h-a-s. which is the abbreviation for Charles.
Yes.

But we'll go into that later. I just wanted to give you a musical lesson, if you'll listen closely. This piece that I'm talking about, is it starts out in the key of -- you're going to play in the key of F.
Yes.
It starts out in the key of F for a little while, then it goes into the key of G for a little while,

then it goes into the key of A flat for a little while, in the middle, which is considered the middle part of the piece. And before it goes out of the middle part it goes into the key of C and then back to F.
And that's to be heard, is it?
That's right. Now, I don't want to go into details on --
Because you can hear that, the chord changes.
Right.
Is that right.
Now, I don't want to go into detail on that because that would take forever and a day.
That's very unusual, isn't it.

Yes. But anybody who knows anything about music knows something to think about. In fact the first time I played the number was much later in my career, and I didn't know the piece. Had a famous jazz musician who wanted to embarrass me, you know, a little friendly, you might say, gesture, in a way, you know.
Yes.
Well, I never could say truthfully whether it was friendly or not. You were-
(inaudible).
Like that --
Being tested.

He asked me if I knew the song and I said, no, I don't know that, but he knew I had a good ear, you know, so he challenged me, he said, oh, you know, he said you can hear it, you know. Now, this was in front of a lot of people you know.
Yes.
It was very embarrassing to me, and I played it so lousy it was a shame. But I never forgot it. Also it was a challenge to me.
But the other people also knew though, didn't they? They knew it was --
Well, there wasn't that many people playing. It was only a saxophone, a drums and bass and piano. So it was --
Yes, it was only the --
There was only two instruments playing lead notes, right.
Yeah, that's right, yes.
I won't call any names but this is also something interesting that goes on, people don't know, inside [jazz]
Yes.
Like you want to know what the coaches talk about you know (whispering), you know, when you
can't read his lips, you know.
Yes, right.
You know.
